 Print this article Reduce font size Increase font size ‘ Dissent over verdict not a criminal act’ 
The Karnataka High Court has quashed a criminal case against 13 people accused of painting slogans criticising a Supreme Court judgment on a public wall, holding that expressing dissatisfaction with a judicial verdict does not, by itself, amount to promoting enmity or outraging religious feelings.
Justice HP Sandesh observed that slogans describing the judgment as a “denial of justice” and calling for a “voice for justice” did not attract offences under Sections 153A and 295A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The court was hearing a petition seeking to quash an FIR registered at Mangalore South Police Station in 2019. The accused had been booked under Sections 153A (promoting enmity between groups), 295A (deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings) and 120B (criminal conspiracy) of the IPC, along with Section 3 of the Karnataka Open Place Disfigurement Act, 1951. The case originated from a suo motu complaint filed by an Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police at Mangalore South Police Station. — BMB
 No malicious intent found in experiment 
The Karnataka High Court has quashed a criminal case against a science content creator who demonstrated the reaction between sodium and water in a video, ruling that the complaint failed to establish the malicious intent required to prosecute him under the Explosive Substances Act, 1908.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj held that sodium, by itself, was not an explosive substance in the context of the case and that the experiment was intended to explain a scientific concept taught to Class 10 students.
The court, however, clarified that it did not approve of the manner in which the experiment was carried out.
The case originated from a complaint filed by a police constable alleging that the petitioner had dropped sodium into a pond at a private farm, causing an explosion that could have posed a danger to people nearby. — BMB
 Man denied relief in homicide charge 
The Karnataka High Court has refused to discharge a Mysuru man from a charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder after his 14-year-old son allegedly drove a car and caused an accident that killed three members of a family, including a five-year-old child.
Justice M Nagaprasanna, while dismissing a criminal petition filed by Nadeem, the boy’s father, observed that parents who knowingly allow minors to drive cannot automatically escape legal scrutiny by citing the child’s age when such conduct results in a fatal accident. — BMB
 Advocate’s conduct sparks contempt action 
The Karnataka High Court has directed its Registrar General to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against a lawyer who refused to file an application to bring the legal representatives of a deceased complainant on record, observing that an advocate’s duty is to assist the court and not insist on an order in his favour.
Justice HP Sandesh passed the order while hearing a petition seeking quashing of an FIR registered under Sections 120B, 200, 404, 419, 420, 421, 423, 424, 426, 464, 467 and 468 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Examining the issue, the bench noted that the applications seeking continuation of the prosecution had been filed by the power of attorney holders of the deceased complainant’s heirs, rather than by the heirs themselves. Dismissing the petition, Justice Sandesh deprecated the lawyer’s conduct, observing that his behaviour was contrary to the principles laid down in the judgments referred to by the court. — BMB GALLERIES View more photos Aero India 2021: 13th edition of air show begins today
